title: The Son Is Worshipped; Faith in God the Father
english: … were saying at his birth: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace” (Luke 2:14).
A summary on worship.

So we have seen him glorified, and we have seen him worshipped too. Both are fitting for God and owed to him, and not to a creature, as the saints cited below write. David, in the ninety-fifth Psalm: “Come, let us worship and fall down before him, and let us weep before the Lord who made us; for he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand” (Psalm 95:6-7). And in the twenty-second: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him; for the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he rules over the nations” (Psalm 22:27-28). What then will they say, who share out the names separately, “God” to the Father and “Lord” to the Son, when they hear here that the Lord is worshipped, that he rules, and that the kingdom is his?

And again, in the ninth Psalm: “And I will worship you, Lord, my strength.” And in the hundred and thirty-second: “Let us worship at the place where his feet stood” (Psalm 132:7). Paul, writing from the Song of Deuteronomy: “And when he brings the Firstborn into the world, he says: And let all the angels of God worship him” (Hebrews 1:6). And the evangelist: “The magi said,” he writes, “We saw his star in the east and have come to worship him” (Matthew 2:2). And again: “Behold,” he says, “a leper came and worshipped him” (Matthew 8:2). And again in Matthew he says: “The wind ceased. And those in the boat worshipped him, saying, Truly you are the Son of God” (Matthew 14:32-33); not, he means, in the way we are sons, who have been called so by a bountiful gift. And: “A certain ruler worshipped him” (Matthew 9:18). And after his resurrection, on the mountain, he says: “The apostles, when they saw him, worshipped him” (Matthew 28:16-17).
On faith in God the Father.

Scripture, then, says many things about the Son that are, to all appearance, greater than what it says about the Father. It declares him Almighty (Revelation 1:8), Maker of the ages (Hebrews 1:2), Creator of all things (John 1:3), true God (1 John 5:20), one who has no God before him (Isaiah 43:10), above all (John 3:31), the great God, God over all (Titus 2:13; Romans 9:5), to whom no other shall be compared (Baruch 3:35), seated with the Father at his right hand (Hebrews 1:3), and dwelling in his bosom (John 1:18). It says that he is eternal life and the true light (1 John 5:20; John 1:9), Lord of all (Acts 10:36), the only Master (Jude 4) and Sovereign, whose peace has no bound but surpasses all understanding (Philippians 4:7), and whose kingdom has no end (Luke 1:33); that salvation is in no one else (Acts 4:12); and that the Father draws the worthy to the Son (John 6:44). Yet the Father is not on that account thought in any respect inferior (God forbid!), nor is his Spirit.

In the same way, when Scripture speaks of the Father in lofty terms, the Only-begotten or the Holy Spirit ought not to be reckoned lesser or unlike. For none of the things just mentioned belongs to any created power, but to the uncreated alone: to create substance, both irrational and rational, out of what is not; to give life; to forgive sins (Mark 2:10); to call creation his own; to know the Father on equal terms, as he is known by him (John 10:15); to work as the Father works (John 5:19); to be in the Father and to have the Father in himself equally (John 14:10); and to be served by angels (Matthew 4:11). And, what surpasses even these, to be attested as only-begotten Son and God, light from light, eternal life, truth and Saviour; to be present everywhere; to have all things established in him; to give the kingdom of heaven and the divine peace, which is his own, ungrudgingly to all (John 14:27); and to grant believers who call on him a sure hold on everlasting salvation.

For those who call the true Son of God and the holy and life-giving Spirit a creature, and not without beginning, do not believe in these hypostases, even if they say they do; and perhaps they do not believe in the Father either. For they transgress the commandment of the Father, who charges: “Hear, my people, and I will speak to you; Israel, I will testify to you, if you will hear me: there shall be no new god among you, nor shall you worship a foreign god” (Psalm 50:7; Psalm 81:8-9), meaning one that once was not, or one of another substance. They transgress “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve” (Deuteronomy 6:13; Matthew 4:10), and “You shall have no other gods besides me” (Exodus 20:3), and “Cursed is everyone who sets his hope on man” (Jeremiah 17:5), that is, on a thing made.
And they transgress this commandment of the Son as well, who says in Matthew: “No one can serve two lords” (Matthew 6:24), that is, two natures or two lordships; and in Paul, to the Romans …

title: The Heretics’ Doxology, and How to Read Scripture’s Theology
english: … writing: “They worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator” (Romans 1:25). And they transgress this command of Moses the lawgiver: “Whoever sacrifices to foreign gods, and not to the Lord alone, shall be stoned” (Exodus 22:20). Now a new and foreign god is one who is not consubstantial with God the Father and who once did not exist.

And those who say, “Glory to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit,” do not glorify the Son or the Spirit of God. For they send up the glory to one, through another, in another; or rather, to neither. And they do injury both to the will of the Father, who says, “My glory I will not give to another” (Isaiah 42:8), meaning to one of another nature, and who wills that the Son be honoured as he is (John 5:23), and to the tradition handed down by the Son. They fare like those who called him Christ with their mouths but struck him with their hands and cried out, “Prophesy to us, Christ: who is it that struck you?” (Matthew 26:68); the same who said, “We believe as Moses and the prophets did,” and yet crucified the very one who had been prophesied.

Since, then, God the Father too goes unheeded together with the only-begotten God, and faith in a creature is useless, able to harm rather than to save, let them consider for themselves whether their faith is free of danger while they deny salvation. For a person must be saved by believing rightly. To be saved is a fine thing, as they say; the rest is another story.

The children of Macedonius, too, do not keep the glory of the Only-begotten, any more than that of the Holy Spirit. They call him of like substance with the Father, and not of the same substance, so that he is understood to be of another substance, a similar one.

So the heretics are left with this choice. Either they must change, in their worship, the name of the Father, since among them he is not truly Father; and that of the only-begotten Son as well; and that of the Spirit of God too, as not being that either (may the holy, venerable and consubstantial Trinity, whom we glorify, pardon us for saying it!). And above all they must change their own name, and no longer be called Christians or spiritual, nor count themselves sons of one kind with their own fathers. Or else they must not estrange the true Son and his Holy Spirit from the Father’s Godhead and glory. For it is the mark of Jews to honour the Father alone, and of Greeks to worship a multitude of demons, great and small, bound by time and of other substances.
How the theology of the Scriptures is to be understood.

I, unworthy as I am, was drawn to take up the cause of the theology of the only-begotten Son and the Holy Spirit, without impairing, even in thought, the ineffable glory of God the Father. For it is well known that, even if he has not been set forth here ahead of both the divine hypostases just named, both hypostases are nevertheless from him by nature and as one in nature with him: that of the Son by way of begetting, that of his Spirit by way of procession. Rather, I was clearing away the ruinous interpretations of the heretics and showing this: that by the very means through which they seem to honour the Father more than Scripture does, they grieve him and outrage his Only-begotten and the Spirit.
More on the same subject.

The orthodox, then, must know this. Even about a small work of God (if one may dare to call any work of God small), those who wish to treat it need words; and works before words; and faith before both of these; and much reverence and the most searching reflection. All this so that, counted worthy through these things to know that even the small thing cannot be captured by the mind, but itself surpasses human efforts of thought without limit (for if it is God’s work, even if it seems small, it is great, as being God’s: “How could anyone take great things with small labours? It is foolish,” they say, “even to want it”), and that much more does the comprehension of the ineffable God himself surpass even the perception of archangels, they may withdraw from perilous inquiries, leaving the knowledge of these things to God alone, and say with the apostle: “I believed, and therefore I spoke” (2 Corinthians 4:13).

And they must understand the theology of the Scriptures in this way. When the Scriptures speak from one person, it is because of the one nature and will; when from both, it is to show the distinct subsistence of the holy and pure Trinity. So when Isaiah says, “I the Lord stretched out the heaven and made firm the earth” (Isaiah 44:24), and again, “I am, and there is no other God besides me” (Isaiah 45:5), it is because of the one Godhead and concord, as was said before. When the Holy Spirit seems not to be mentioned, it is because he is included together with God, whose Spirit he is. When the mystical teaching …

title: How Scripture Speaks of the Three; the Incomprehensible Trinity
english: … the Master, in handing it down, says, “Baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19), it is because the hypostases are equal in honour, equal in might and consubstantial, and yet clearly distinct. When what is said in one place of God the Father is recorded elsewhere of the Only-begotten or of the Holy Spirit, it is for the reasons given before. When the Scriptures teach in different ways that both hypostases do the same works, the same activity, it is for the reason stated before.

When, though each hypostasis was able to create and make all things, God the Father was pleased that all things should come into being through the Son, who is God, and be sanctified through the Holy Spirit, it is because of the one will of the Trinity, and to show that every good thing is supplied from it, and so that we may send up to it a common and equal thanksgiving and doxology.

When the Scriptures use the same names for the blessed Trinity, such as “God”, “Lord”, “Holy”, “Righteous”, “Good” and the like (except that “the Father” is alone and always Father, “the true Son and God” is Son and God without beginning, and “the Holy Spirit” is, without beginning, one and the same Spirit of God), it is because of their communion in nature and kingdom and all things; and this holds of the Trinity alone. When they speak in veiled terms, it is because the mystery of the faith is always guarded, revealed to the faithful alone. When they say that God the Father begot, that the Son, the Word, was begotten, and that the Holy Spirit proceeds, it is so that we may understand, as befits God, that they came forth from the hypostasis of the Father without beginning and without passion, not as creatures do, and that they are united.

When he says, “The Father who sent me is greater than I” (John 14:28), and whatever else is thought too small for the Godhead, it is because of his ineffable and voluntary economy for our sake and on your behalf. For in the Godhead neither smallness nor not being everywhere has any place.

When the Son says, “My Father has given me a commandment, what I should say and what I should speak, and I have not spoken from myself” (John 12:49), and of the Holy Spirit, “He will not speak from himself” (John 16:13), and the like, it is because of the concord of the divine hypostases, and because the teachings and gifts of the blessed Trinity are common, not at odds with one another as those of men are.
That the Holy Trinity is incomprehensible.

Those who strive to be a temple, worthy in some measure, of the Holy Spirit who dwells in the faithful (1 Corinthians 6:19), as men who once for all have the inaccessible light (1 Timothy 6:16) shining within them, glorify with equal honour, as the Master decreed in the mystagogy of baptism, the self-existent God and Father; the beloved and only-begotten Son, the Word, who is from him and coexists with him; and the Holy Spirit just named, who alone proceeded from his hypostasis, without beginning and without interval.

They do not disbelieve the consubstantiality of the Trinity, but neither do they inquire into the manner of begetting and of procession, or the difference between them. For this is unknown even to the ministering powers of heaven, ineffable, and fearful to ponder. So too is how the Holy Trinity co-subsists with itself without beginning, ever the same and in the same way; and how, seated on the eternal throne, it can look upon the depths, be heard while it is silent, and hear those who are silent; and know what is to come before it is done; and bring all things into being by a word, and faster than a word, by willing alone; and, before anyone has searched his own heart (only let it be in faith and righteousness), give at once its verdict on the request; and fit for everyone the right moment for kindness; and be slow to anger but ready to do good; and be provoked by our offences, yet remit the punishment out of its own love for mankind.

More than that, it is incomprehensible how it has one will, and speaks and bestows in common, as one; and how it looks not so much to the good health of bodies as to the contrite heart itself. And this too: how it is invisible and not to be grasped even by the eyes of the seraphim, not to be contained by word or place; without parts in its power, beyond touch, without size, untaught, without breadth, without form; all-surveying, all-hearing, and the hope of all; brighter by far than heavenly light, higher than every height beyond what can be said, and more intelligent than every mind by an infinite measure.

For how could the things of the Trinity fail to be incomprehensible to all, when it is itself the author of all things and highest above every intellectual creation, and indeed every intelligible one? Beyond it there is nothing whatever, but all things …
